latin: Congriō, domō Euclīonis ērumpit. — Optātī cīvēs<sup>1</sup>, populārēs<sup>2</sup>, incolae, accolae, advenae, omnēs...
Datē viam quā fugere<sup>3</sup> liceat, facite tōtae platēae<sup>4</sup> pateant<sup>5</sup>.
Neque ego unquam nisi hodiē ad Bacchās venī in Bacchānal<sup>6</sup> coquinātum<sup>7</sup>.
Ita mē miserum et meōs discipulōs fustibus<sup>8</sup> male contudērunt.
Tōtus doleō atque oppidō<sup>9</sup> periī*, ita mē iste senex habuit gymnasium.
Neque ligna ego usquam<sup>10</sup> gentium praebērī vīdī pulchrius...
Attat, periī hercle ego miser; adest*, sequitur!
Sciō quam rem geram: hoc ipse magister mē docuit.
Eucliō. — Redī! Quō fugis nunc? Tēne, tenē!
Cong. — Quid, stolidē, clāmās?
Eucl. — Quia ad trēsvirōs<sup>11</sup> jam ego dēferam* nōmen tuum.
Cong. — Quam ob rem<sup>12</sup>?
Eucl. — Quia cultrum habēs.
Cong. — Coquum decet*.
Eucl. — Quid comminātus es<sup>13</sup> mihi?
Cong. — Istud male factum arbitror, quia nōn latus fōdī.
Eucl. — Homō nullust (= nūllus est) tē scelestior<sup>14</sup> quī vīvat hodiē!

Datē viam quā fúgere<sup>3</sup> líceat, fácite tōtae platḗae<sup>4</sup> páteant<sup>5</sup>.
Neque ego unquam nisi hódiē ad Bacchās venī in Bacchā́nal<sup>6</sup> coquinā́tum<sup>7</sup>.
Ita mē míserum et meōs discípulōs fústibus<sup>8</sup> male contudḗrunt.
Tōtus dóleō atque óppidō<sup>9</sup> périī*, ita mē iste senex hábuit gymnásium.
Neque ligna ego usquam<sup>10</sup> géntium praebḗrī vīdī púlchrius...
Attat, périī hercle ego miser; adest*, séquitur!
Sciō quam rem geram: hoc ipse magíster mē dócuit.
Eúcliō. — Redī! Quō fugis nunc? Tēne, tenē!
Cong. — Quid, stólidē, clāmās?
Eucl. — Quia ad trḗsvirōs<sup>11</sup> jam ego dḗferam* nōmen tuum.
Cong. — Quam ob rem<sup>12</sup>?
Eucl. — Quia cultrum habēs.
Cong. — Coquum decet*.
Eucl. — Quid comminā́tus es<sup>13</sup> mihi?
Cong. — Istud male factum árbitror, quia nōn latus fōdī.
Eucl. — Homō nullust (= nūllus est) tē sceléstior<sup>14</sup> quī vīvat hódiē!
english: Congrio [bursts out] of Euclio's house. — Dear citizens, fellow countrymen, inhabitants [of the quarter] (neighbours) [and of the neighbourhood], foreigners [all of you]...
[Open] (give) the road [by which I may be allowed to flee], make all the avenues open.
[Never up to today] (nor I ever unless today) have I been to the Bacchantes to do the cooking in [such] a Bacchanal (see N. 6).
[Poor me!] (me miserum)! [In what a state] (ita... male) [they have put me] and my helpers! [they have us] beaten black and blue!
I hurt [all over] (whole) and I am completely done for, [so much has this cursed old man turned me into a boxing ring] (thus me this old man has had [as] gymnasium).
And never [have I seen] anywhere [in the world] (of nations) [wood] (ligna, pl. n.) [supplied] more [beautifully]...
Hey! Damn it! I'm done for! [Woe is me]; he is there, he [is following me]!
I know what [I'm going] to do: [he himself the master taught me it].
Eucl. — Come back! Where are you running to now? (Hold-[him], hold-[him])! [stop him]!
Cong. — [Why] are you shouting? Imbecile!
Eucl. — Because I'm going straight away to [lodge a complaint at the police] (will give your name to the triumvirs).
Cong. — For what reason?
Eucl. — Because you have a knife.
Cong. — [For] a cook, [that's quite normal] (it is fitting).
Eucl. — [Why] did you threaten [me]?
Cong. — [I was quite wrong] (that badly done I think) not to pierce your side (this badly done I think, because I have not pierced the flank).
Eucl. — [You are the greatest scoundrel in the world] (man none is than you more wicked who lives today)!

footnotes: Optatus, -a, -um (past participle of optare, to choose, to wish), is often used in an apostrophe: optati amici, dear friends. Civis, -is, m., the citizen.

Popularis, -e, adj., relating to the people (populus). Used as a noun, it means fellow citizen, compatriot. The three other nouns of the sentence present no difficulties. Note that they are masculines of the 1st declension.
Fugio, -is, -ere, fugi, v.i., to flee; but fugo, -as, -are, v.t., to put to flight: Euclio Congrionem fugat, E. puts C. to flight; but Congrio Euclionis verbera fugit, C. flees E.'s blows.
Platea, -ae, f., public square, avenue, landing strip (E. 67, P. 9).

Pateo, -es, -ere, -ui, to be open; here in the subjunctive with ut understood. Other sense: to be clear, to be evident. To this verb corresponds the form patesco, -is, -ere, patui, to open, to unveil oneself.

Baccha, -ae, f., Bacchante, priestess of Bacchus, god of wine and drunkenness. Bacchanal, -alis, n., place consecrated to this god, where the Bacchanalia, -ium, pl. n., feasts of wine, were held, which, as one guesses, were celebrated in a lively way!
Coquina, -ae, f., kitchen; whence coquinare (supine coquinatum), to do the cooking; one also says culina (L. 81, P. 11); to cook is said coquere (cf. L. 65, N. 5) and cook, coquus (L. 81, P. 11).
Fustis, -is, m., cut wood, cudgel (cf. French fustiger).
Oppido, adv., completely. The kinship with oppidum, -i, n., the (fortified) town is doubtful.
Ne... usquam or nusquam, nowhere; likewise, higher up, ne (que)... unquam = nunquam, never.

Tresviri (gen. triumvirorum), m. pl., the triumvirs, of whom it is a question here, were charged with the policing of prisons at that time. There were other sorts of triumvirs: the best known were first Caesar, Pompey and Crassus, then Antony, Octavian and Lepidus, whose triumvirate (lit. group of three men) was established in 43 B.C.
Quam ob rem, for what thing, why (can be written in a single word). Ob + acc., because of.
Comminari, as well as minari = to threaten (v. dep.). Fodio, -is, -ere, fodi, fossum, to pierce, to dig.

Scelestus, -a, -um, criminal, villain (scelus, -eris, n., crime); here in the comparative; its complement te is in the ablative (without quam). Forget immediately the translation «crapule», for this last word literally means, like the Latin crapula, excess of drink or of good cheer.
comments: Vhiskeum: the Latin v is pronounced like the English w. — Verber, -eris, n., stick, whip; in the plural, verbera (pl. of verberum), blows of the same instrument. Verberare, to beat, to whip. Verbero, -onis, m., scoundrel (accustomed to the whip). Lacus, -us, m.: dative and ablative plural lacubus. Likewise acus, the needle, and a few other nouns of the 4th declension have the dative and ablative plural in ubus instead of ibus (cf. E. 33). Vetus, -eris, contrary to most adjectives of the 3rd declension, does not make its ablative singular in i but in e (likewise dives, divitis, and pauper, pauperis, as well as comparatives (cf. L. 39, N. 7).

latin: Quā ratiōne pōtum quī «vhiskeum» apud anglōs vocātur tam cōpiōsē bibere assuēfactus es*?
Explicābō tibi: imprīmīs cum aquā; posteā sine aquā; dēnique sīcut aquam.
Quō tam celeriter vādis?
Domum, nam māter verbera mihi pollicita est.
Ego vērō nōn intellegō cūr sīc properēs.
Ut domum perveniam antequam pater redeat*: ille enim multō validius verberat.
Olīva glōriātur quod lacus in patriā sua piscibus sunt refertissimī:
«Edepol, inquit, in hīs lacubus tam multī sunt piscēs ut, aqua tantum remōtā, apprehendī possint*».
Marius autem: «Quod nihil est, inquit, Massiliae tot sunt piscēs in Portū Vetēre ut removendī sint ad aquam nāvigandī causā līberandam».
latinAccented: Quā ratiṓne pōtum quī «vhískeum» apud anglōs vocā́tur tam cōpiṓsē bíbere assuēfáctus es*?
Explicā́bō tibi: imprī́mīs cum aquā; pósteā sine aquā; dḗnique sīcut aquam.
Quō tam celériter vādis?
Domum, nam māter vérbera mihi pollícita est.
Ego vērō nōn intéllegō cūr sīc próperēs.
Ut domum pervéniam ántequam pater rédeat*: ille enim multō valídius vérberat.
Olī́va glōriā́tur quod lacus in pátriā sua píscibus sunt refertíssimī:
«Édepol, inquit, in hīs lácubus tam multī sunt piscēs ut, aqua tantum remṓtā, apprehéndī possint*».
Márius autem: «Quod nihil est, inquit, Massíliae tot sunt piscēs in Portū Vetḗre ut removéndī sint ad aquam nāvigándī causā līberándam».
english: How did you get into the habit of drinking so copiously [the] drink which is called «whisky» among the English?
I'll explain it to you: first with water, then without water, finally like water.
Where are you going so fast?
Home, because Mummy has promised me a spanking.
So, I don't understand why you are hurrying like that.
To get home before my father comes back: he hits much harder.
Olive boasts [that] the lakes in his country are very abundant in fish:
«By Pollux, he says, in these lakes the fish are so numerous that [it is enough] to lift the water [for them to be caught] (water only having been removed, to be seized they can)».
But Marius: «That's nothing, he says, in Marseille there are so many fish in the Old Port that they must be removed to make the water free [for] navigation (with a view to sailing)».
